title: Block B close: the generation
hookLine: slaves and merchants, poets and nurses, women and men, all of them learners

lines: A MERCHANT, A CALLER, A SEEKER.
A POET, A NURSE, A TEACHER.
cards: Lay them out on a table like photographs. A merchant who spent his wealth buying people out of slavery. A man of Abyssinian descent who had been one of those people, calling the prayer.
A Persian who traveled from teacher to teacher looking for the truth. A poet. A nurse in a tent.
A woman who taught writing. A woman who asked for a day. A shepherd who became a reciter.
A man from Yemen who stayed home with his mother. Call that pile one generation, and someone might ask what holds it together.

teach.b: Today the block on the companions closes. It opened with a question: who is a companion?
A sahabi, in the common Sunni definition, is someone who met the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, as a believer, and died a believer.
That's a wide door, and nobody came through it for their background. The first circle: Abu Bakr and his purchases, Umar walking at night, Uthman and the well of Rumah, Ali and his words.
The mothers of the believers: Khadijah, Aisha the scholar, Hafsah keeping the pages, Umm Salamah and the others. The family: Fatimah and her hands, Hasan the peacemaker, Husayn.
Then Bilal, Salman, Abu Dharr, Ammar, Mus'ab, Zayd, Usamah, Umm Ayman. The reciters: Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy, Zayd ibn Thabit, Mu'adh.

And this last stretch: Abu Hurayrah and Anas, Nusaybah at Uhud, Asma and her two belts, Rufaydah's tent, al-Shifa teaching writing, Umm Sulaym, Hassan the poet, Ka'b who told the truth, Suhayb, Khabbab the blacksmith, Abu Ayyub the host, Sa'd, Abu Musa, Hudhayfah and Salim.
And Uways, who by that definition was not a companion at all, since he never met the Prophet, yet whose story sits among theirs. So what holds them together?
Story after story, someone is learning: asking a question, memorizing a verse, standing behind whoever knew the most Qur'an. Read this way, they look like a generation of students.

teach.h: REMEMBERED IN MORE THAN ONE WAY.
teach.b: One more honest thing: Sunni and Shia Muslims hold different views about some companions, especially around what happened after the Prophet's death.
The next block begins there, with each telling in its own words.

how: Muslims retell the lives of the companions in sermons, classes and family storytelling, and say 'may God be pleased with him' or 'with her' after a companion's name.

o: any Muslim who lived in Medina in the Prophet's time
someone who met the Prophet as a believer and died a believer
one of the ten promised Paradise by the Prophet

s: the companions all came from the same class and background
merchants and freed slaves, poets and nurses, men and women, from Mecca, Medina, Abyssinia, Persia and Yemen.
a common Sunni definition: a companion met the Prophet as a believer and died a believer
that's the wide door this block began with.
all Muslims remember every companion in exactly the same way
Sunni and Shia Muslims hold different views about some companions. the next block begins there.

games.q: someone hands you the whole block's stories and asks what holds this generation together. what do you answer?
o: they all came from noble families.
nearly every story has someone learning.
games.why: asking, memorizing, requesting a day, asking about harm. read this way, the companions look like a generation of students.

practice: Write down every companion from this block you can recall, and next to each name one thing: a belt, a tent, a well, a pipe, a mother. Read the list back slowly.
If you pray, you can add the words Muslims say after a companion's name: may God be pleased with them.

wordCard.voice: Sahabi, a companion of the Prophet: someone who met him as a believer and died a believer. This block's close: a generation of very different people, held together by learning and faith. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a companion of the Prophet; plural sahabah.

carryVoice: Your line: ordinary people, extraordinary faith. Very different lives, one generation of learners. Day eight hundred sixty-two.
